item.title: Comprehensive profiling of brain dynamics during anesthesia across phylogeny
item.headline: Under anesthesia, brain signals lose persistence and coordination
item.summary: Across six species, measured neural signals became less persistent and synchronized under anesthesia. This shared pattern is not a universal test of consciousness.

evidence.question: Do different anesthetics produce shared changes in neural activity?
evidence.method: Compared 6,827 signal features using mammalian fMRI and zebrafish/nematode calcium imaging; the human sample included 15 healthy men.
evidence.limitations: Small samples, different drugs, doses, and recording methods limit comparisons.

explainer.finding: Slow signals retained less similarity to their recent past, and activity across regions became less coordinated.
explainer.method: Researchers compared awake and anesthetized recordings, with permutation checks for chance consistency.
explainer.meaning: In two macaques, targeted thalamic stimulation restored behavioral responsiveness and shifted signals toward the awake pattern despite continued anesthesia.
explainer.limits: Responsiveness does not directly measure subjective experience. These slow imaging signals also differ from fast electrical brain rhythms.
